title: The Best Air Quality Monitors for Testing Your Air Indoors and Out
gist: A WIRED buying guide to consumer air quality monitors (IQAir AirVisual Pro, PurpleAir Zen, Temtop S1, Airthings View Plus), framed around rising wildfire smoke exposure, with pricing from $28-$330 and a note that low-cost consumer sensors are less accurate than professional-grade equipment.

themes.theme: Wildfire smoke as a durable demand driver

insights.claim: The article frames rising wildfire frequency and intensity from climate change as the core reason consumer demand for home air quality monitors has grown, since wildfire smoke exposure 'can't always be smelled or seen.'
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: Climate-driven wildfire frequency is a structural, recurring (not one-off) demand tailwind for the consumer air-quality-monitoring and air-purifier product category.

insights.claim: Consumer-grade air quality monitors in the sub-$200 price range are described as cheaper but less accurate and harder to calibrate than professional-grade equipment used by experts, though independent study found the WIRED-tested AirVisual Pro and PurpleAir sensors performed well.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: A meaningful accuracy gap between consumer and professional sensors is a segmentation signal for the category -- premium brands with independently validated sensors (IQAir, PurpleAir) may command durable pricing power over cheap unvalidated competitors.

insights.claim: PurpleAir's Zen monitor ($299) can optionally link to PurpleAir's crowdsourced Real-Time Air Quality Map, contributing citizen-scientist data; the reviewer notes surprisingly dense existing monitor coverage even at the neighborhood/block level in New York City and Brooklyn.
insights.speaker: Molly Higgins
insights.so_what: PurpleAir has built a de facto crowdsourced hyperlocal air-quality data network from consumer hardware sales, a data-moat model that a hardware-only competitor would struggle to replicate quickly.
